drugRefs.why: Fluoroquinolones achieve excellent prostatic tissue penetration, which is essential since many antibiotics with good urinary concentration do not adequately penetrate prostatic tissue; prolonged duration (longer than typical UTI) reduces the risk of chronic prostatitis.

drugRefs.coverage: Alternative with reasonable prostatic penetration where local E. coli susceptibility is favorable.

drugRefs.regimenLabel: Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin/Doxycycline (if STI risk in younger sexually active men)
drugRefs.dose: Ceftriaxone 500 mg-1g IM/IV single dose + Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h x 10-14 days
drugRefs.coverage: Specifically covers gonococcal and chlamydial causes in the appropriate epidemiological context, which require an entirely different regimen than typical uropathogen-directed therapy.

coverageMatrix.completeness: Fluoroquinolones provide the most reliable combination of organism coverage and prostatic tissue penetration for typical uropathogen-related prostatitis.
gaps: Enterococcus and STI pathogens not covered by standard fluoroquinolone therapy — assess risk factors and adjust accordingly.

stewardship.deescalation: Narrow to the most targeted oral agent once urine culture and susceptibility are available; complete the full extended duration even with early symptomatic improvement to reduce chronic prostatitis risk.

drugs.drug: Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin/Doxycycline (if STI risk in younger sexually active men)
drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 500 mg-1g IM/IV single dose + Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h x 10-14 days
drugs.coverage: Specifically covers gonococcal and chlamydial causes in the appropriate epidemiological context, which require an entirely different regimen than typical uropathogen-directed therapy.

framework: Duration is intentionally longer (2-4 weeks) than typical UTI/pyelonephritis given the risk of chronic bacterial prostatitis with undertreatment — do not apply standard UTI duration logic here.
Specifically ask about sexual history/risk factors in younger men, since STI-related prostatitis requires entirely different therapy (and partner treatment) than typical uropathogen-related disease.
Avoid vigorous prostatic massage/instrumentation in the acute setting given bacteremia risk; gentle digital rectal exam for diagnostic purposes is acceptable.
